title: Henselian normalization and normal completion of a quasi-excellent local ring
statement: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a reduced quasi-excellent Noetherian local ring, with ordinary henselization $H=R^h$ [def-weil-pbc-henselization-at-prime], [def-exc-excellent-ring], [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Then $H$ is reduced, Noetherian, excellent and henselian [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], and $\dim H=\dim R$. Its componentwise normalization [def-weil-pbc-reduced-normalization] is a finite product $\prod_{a=1}^r B_a$ of normal excellent henselian Noetherian local domains. The map $\coprod_a\operatorname{Spec}B_a\to\operatorname{Spec}H$ is finite and surjective and is an isomorphism over a dense open containing every generic point. Each $\dim B_a\leq\dim H$. For any normal excellent Noetherian local domain $B$, its maximal-ideal completion $\widehat B$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion] is a normal Noetherian local domain, and $B\to\widehat B$ is faithfully flat. A nowhere dense closed subset of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ has nowhere dense inverse image in $\operatorname{Spec}H$, in each $\operatorname{Spec}B_a$, and in $\operatorname{Spec}\widehat B_a$. Here normal means integrally closed in the fraction field; finite means finite as a module; and dimension is Krull dimension [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring].

source.place: Expose I Theorem 8.1 and following paragraph (p.16), Corollary 6.3(ii) and Proposition 6.2 (p.14); III Proposition 6.2, first three reductions (pp.43--44). Dimension of henselization: Stacks more-algebra.tex Tag 06LK, lemma-henselization-dimension; reducedness: Tag 06DH, lemma-henselization-reduced; normal completion: Tag 0C23, lemma-completion-normal-local-ring. The normalization is finite birational, and the henselian finite algebra decomposition gives its local factors.

proof.text: Identify $R_{\mathfrak m}=R$, since all denominators outside $\mathfrak m$ are units. First identify ordinary henselization with the henselization of the pair $(R,\mathfrak m)$. Write $(C,J)$ for the latter. The pair-henselization theorem gives $J=\mathfrak mC$, $C/J=R/\mathfrak m$ and a henselian pair. The henselian factorization criterion puts $J$ in the Jacobson radical. Since $C/J$ is a field, $J$ is the unique maximal ideal of $C$. Thus $C$ is henselian local and $R\to C$ is local. For a local map $R\to T$ with $T$ henselian local, the pair universal property gives a unique $R$-map $C\to T$; it is local because it carries $J=\mathfrak mC$ into the maximal ideal of $T$. Hence $C$ and $H$ have the same ordinary local universal property. The unique local maps between them compose to the identities by uniqueness, identifying $C=H$, $J=\mathfrak mH$, and $H/\mathfrak mH=R/\mathfrak m$.

source.place: Tag 0A02, lemma-henselization; local comparison by universal properties; algebra.tex Tag 04GG, lemma-characterize-henselian

proof.text: The Noetherian pair-henselization theorem applied with $I=\mathfrak m$ now gives that $H$ is Noetherian, $R\to H$ is flat, and $\widehat R\cong\widehat H$. It also identifies $H$ with a filtered colimit of etale $R$-algebras. Each such algebra is reduced by etale preservation of reducedness, using the reducedness criterion on affine sections. This implies that $H$ is reduced: if $x^n=0$ in the colimit, represent $x$ at a stage and pass to a later stage at which its $n$th power is zero; reducedness at that stage makes its image, and therefore $x$, zero.
Apply invariance of dimension under completion to the two Noetherian local rings $R$ and $H$. The completion isomorphism in Step 2 gives $\dim R=\dim\widehat R=\dim\widehat H=\dim H$.

source.place: Tag 06LK, lemma-henselization-dimension; alternative completion comparison using more-algebra.tex Tag 07NV, lemma-completion-dimension

proof.text: The ordinary henselization map is ind-etale, hence weakly etale. Quasi-excellence of $R$ supplies the G-ring and J-2 properties and, by quasi-excellent implies Nagata, the Nagata property. The weakly etale G-ring ascent theorem and the weakly etale Nagata/J-2 ascent theorem apply to the Noetherian rings $R,H$. They give that $H$ is a G-ring and J-2, hence quasi-excellent. Universal catenarity is proved below, rather than assumed here.

source.place: Expose I Theorem 8.1(i),(iii) and following henselization paragraph, p.16

proof.text: Apply quasi-excellent implies Nagata to $H$. Enumerate its finitely many minimal primes $\mathfrak p_a$ and set $A_a=H/\mathfrak p_a$, $K_a=\operatorname{Frac}(A_a)$ and $B_a$ equal to the integral closure of $A_a$ in $K_a$. The normalization affine-chart theorem identifies the componentwise normalization of $\operatorname{Spec}H$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(\prod_a B_a)$, with structural map $h\mapsto(h\bmod\mathfrak p_a)_a$. By the Nagata definition each $A_a$ is Japanese; taking the degree-one extension $K_a/K_a$ in that definition makes $B_a$ finite over $A_a$, and therefore finite over $H$. The integral-closure theorem makes each $B_a$ a normal domain.

source.place: Expose I Proposition 6.2, p.14; III Proposition 6.2, normalization paragraph, p.44; Stacks Tag 07QV and the affine normalization construction

proof.text: Apply finite-over-henselian decomposition to each finite $H$-algebra $B_a$. Since $B_a$ is a nonzero domain, the product can have only one nonzero local factor: two would give an idempotent different from $0$ and $1$. Thus each $B_a$ is henselian local and $H\to B_a$ is local. A finite module algebra is of finite type, so the finite-type Noetherian and G-ring ascent theorems give that $B_a$ is Noetherian and a G-ring. Normal-domain localization shows it is also a normal ring in the local-at-every-prime sense.

For each $B_a$, its completion is Noetherian and local by the completion theorems. As $B_a$ is a local G-ring, the definition makes $B_a\to\widehat B_a$ regular. Its fibres are regular rings, hence normal rings by regular implies normal. Apply flat ascent of normality with normal fibres: the source and target are Noetherian, the map is flat, all its fibres are normal, and its source is normal by Step 6. It follows that $\widehat B_a$ is a normal ring. A normal local ring is a normal domain: its localization at its maximal ideal is a normal domain by the definition, and that localization is the ring itself since every element outside the maximal ideal is a unit. The completion map is faithfully flat by the local-completion theorem.

source.place: Tag 0C23, lemma-completion-normal-local-ring, proof via normal-fibre ascent; algebra.tex Tag 00MC

proof.text: Fix $a$. The quotient $A_a$ is Noetherian local, and $A_a\hookrightarrow B_a$ is injective and finite; the maximal ideal of $B_a$ contracts to that of $A_a$ by Step 6. The completion $\widehat A_a$ is flat over $A_a$, so tensoring this injection gives an injection $\widehat A_a\hookrightarrow\widehat A_a\otimes_{A_a}B_a$ by the definition of flatness. The finite-extension completion theorem identifies the latter ring with $\widehat B_a$: there is just one prime over the maximal ideal, because $B_a$ is local and integral over $A_a$ (a prime over a maximal ideal in an integral extension is maximal). Consequently $\widehat A_a$ is a domain, as it embeds in the domain $\widehat B_a$.

source.place: Expose I Corollary 6.3(ii), proof, p.14: henselian component normalization and integral completion; finite-extension comparison in Stacks algebra.tex

proof.text: Completion of the quotient $H\twoheadrightarrow A_a$ identifies $\widehat H/\mathfrak p_a\widehat H$ with $\widehat A_a$. Step 8 shows this is a domain; its spectrum has a single irreducible component, and so is equidimensional. Apply the formal catenarity criterion to $H$: these assertions hold for every minimal prime $\mathfrak p_a$, and hence $H$ is universally catenary. Together with Step 4 this proves that $H$ is excellent. Each $B_a$ is a finite type $H$-algebra, so excellence of finite type algebras makes each $B_a$ excellent.

source.place: Expose I Corollary 6.3(ii), proof, p.14; XIV Proposition 1.3.2, p.209; Stacks formal catenarity criterion and Tag 07QU

proof.text: Now apply excellent-normalization preparation to $X=\operatorname{Spec}H$. Steps 2 and 9 verify that it is reduced Noetherian excellent. Its normalization is the one identified in Step 5. The cited theorem gives that $\coprod_a\operatorname{Spec}B_a\to\operatorname{Spec}H$ is finite and surjective and is an isomorphism over a dense open containing every generic point. This uses the already proved excellence, so there is no use of normalization finiteness to assume universal catenarity in Step 9.

source.place: III Proposition 6.2, normalization paragraph, p.44; Stacks morphisms.tex Tags 035S, 035Q and 0BAJ

proof.text: The map $A_a\hookrightarrow B_a$ is integral and injective, so $\dim B_a=\dim A_a$. The quotient spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}A_a$ is the closed subspace $V(\mathfrak p_a)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}H$. Equivalently, lifting a strict chain of primes along the quotient gives a strict chain in $H$; hence $\dim A_a\leq\dim H$. This proves the required bound for every factor, without assuming the components of $H$ have equal dimensions.

source.place: Tag 00OK, lemma-integral-sub-dim-equal, and prime correspondence for a quotient

proof.text: For the separately quantified normal excellent Noetherian local domain $B$, apply the same completion argument as in Step 7: excellence supplies the G-ring property; normal-domain localization gives normality at every prime; regular formal fibres are normal by regular implies normal; and the Noetherian flat-normal-fibre ascent theorem gives normality of $\widehat B$. The completion-locality and Noetherianity theorems apply to $B$, so this normal ring is a local domain by localization at its maximal ideal. Local-completion faithful flatness gives the asserted $B\to\widehat B$. No henselian hypothesis on this arbitrary $B$ is used.

Let $Z\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R$ be nowhere dense and closed. In a Noetherian spectrum this means it contains no minimal prime: irreducible components are the closures of their generic minimal primes. Any nonempty open contains one of these generic points. Conversely, if a closed set contains a component, deleting the other finitely many components exhibits a nonempty ambient open in that closed set. These observations give the equivalence. Flat going down for $R\to H$ shows that every minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ of $H$ contracts to a minimal prime of $R$: a strictly smaller prime below its contraction would lift to a prime strictly below $\mathfrak q$. Thus $Z_H$ contains no minimal prime of $H$, and is nowhere dense. The generic prime $(0)$ of each $B_a$ contracts to $\mathfrak p_a$ in $H$ by its embedding $H/\mathfrak p_a\hookrightarrow B_a$; hence the inverse image $Z_a$ misses that generic point. Being a proper closed subset of an irreducible spectrum it is nowhere dense. Finally apply flat going down to $B_a\to\widehat B_a$: its minimal prime contracts to the unique minimal prime $(0)$ of $B_a$. Therefore the closed inverse image of $Z_a$ misses the generic point of $\operatorname{Spec}\widehat B_a$ and is nowhere dense as well.
